paragraphs: Friend, here's what I see in this passage. Abram doesn't grab. He has the bigger claim, the God who called him and the family seniority, and he still says, "Please let there be no contention between you and me." He gives Lot first pick, and he does it because "we are kinsmen" (Genesis 13:8-9). Peace with the people you love is worth more than winning the argument, and Abram acts like he knows it.

Now look at Lot. He looks out, sees a plain that is "well watered," and takes it (Genesis 13:10-11). The writer tells us the men of Sodom "were wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD," and Lot pitches his tent toward them anyway (Genesis 13:12-13). I think Lot was looking at what the land could give him, and he never asked what the neighbors might cost him. Friend, a good-looking choice and a good choice are not always the same cookie.

And here's the part I love. Abram gave up first pick, and after Lot leaves, the LORD speaks: "Now lift up your eyes," because "all the land that you see, I will give to you and your offspring forever" (Genesis 13:14-15). Abram didn't have to hold on tight, because God was the one holding his future. So Abram moves his tent and builds an altar to the LORD (Genesis 13:18). Baker, when you let go of something for peace, you're not left empty-handed, because God is still the One who gives.
